questions.knowledge_point: Integrating Expressions Using the Double-Angle Formula for Cosine
questions.worked_solution:
Here, we use the double-angle formula for cosine:

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .
$$

Letting $\theta =2x,$ we get

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡4x={cos}^{2}⁡2x-{sin}^{2}⁡2x.
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /24}({cos}^{2}⁡2x-{sin}^{2}⁡2x)\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /24}\operatorname{cos}⁡4x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡4x}{4}{|}_{0}^{\pi /24} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\cdot \frac{\pi }{24})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\cdot 0)] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})-\operatorname{sin}⁡0] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\frac{1}{2}-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Integrating Using the Squared Cosine Variant of the Cosine Double-Angle Formula
questions.worked_solution:
Here, we use the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta $ term, given by

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta =2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -1.
$$

 

Rearranging, we have

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta +1).
$$

Letting $\theta =2x$, we have

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡2x=\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+1).
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (5-8{cos}^{2}⁡2x)\text{d}x & =\int [5-8\cdot \frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+1)]\text{d}x \\  & =\int [5-4(\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+1)]\text{d}x \\  & =\int (1-4\operatorname{cos}⁡4x)\text{d}x \\  & =x-4(\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡4x)+C \\  & =x-\operatorname{sin}⁡4x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Let's recall the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${sin}^{2}$ term: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2x=1-2{sin}^{2}⁡x
$$

We can now integrate as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (1-2{sin}^{2}⁡x)\text{d}x & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+C\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069699/assets/77004c9040818fbc254b9564b9c5821536ef65fcc77f6765b56d2e8524c24ed4.png)

Find the area $A$ of the region in the $xy$-plane that is bounded by the curve $y=6{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{3})+2{sin}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{3})+1,$ the $x$-axis and the lines $x=-\frac{3\pi }{2}$ and $x=0,$ as shown above. Do not round the answer

$A=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The area of the region is given by

$$
A={\int }_{-3\pi /2}^{0}(6{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{3})+2{sin}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{3})+1)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Recall  ${cos}^{2}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x=1,$ so we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}6{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{3})+2{sin}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{3})+1 & =4{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{3})+2({sin}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{3})+{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{3}))+1 \\  & =4{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{3})+3.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we use the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${cos}^{2}⁡x$ term, given by

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2x=2{cos}^{2}⁡x-1.
$$

 

Rearranging, we have

$$
2{cos}^{2}⁡x=\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+1.
$$

Hence, the area of the region is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{-3\pi /2}^{0}(4{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{3})+3)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-3\pi /2}^{0}(2(cos\,(\frac{2x}{3})+1)+3)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-3\pi /2}^{0}(2cos\,(\frac{2x}{3})+5)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(3sin\,(\frac{2x}{3})+5x)\,|}_{-3\pi /2}^{0} \\  & =(3\operatorname{sin}⁡0+5\cdot 0)-(3sin\,(\frac{2}{3}\cdot (-\frac{3\pi }{2}))+5(-\frac{3\pi }{2})) \\  & =(0+0)-(3\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi )-\frac{15\pi }{2}) \\  & =(0)-(0-\frac{15\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{15\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Integrating Using the Squared Sine Variant of the Cosine Double-Angle Formula
questions.worked_solution:
Let's recall the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${sin}^{2}$ term: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta =1-2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .
$$

We can rearrange the above formula as

$$
1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta =2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .
$$

Letting $\theta =\frac{x}{6},$ we have

$$
1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{3})=2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{x}{6}).
$$

We can now integrate as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{3\pi }^{6\pi }6{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{x}{6})\,\text{d}x & =3{\int }_{3\pi }^{6\pi }2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{x}{6})\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{3\pi }^{6\pi }[1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{3})]\text{d}x \\  & =3{[x-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{3})]}_{3\pi }^{6\pi } \\  & =3[6\pi -3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{6\pi }{3})-(3\pi -3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{3}))] \\  & =3[6\pi -3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )-(3\pi -3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi ))] \\  & =3(6\pi -3\pi ) \\  & =9\pi .\end{aligned}
$$
